title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
authors: Davi Castro-Silva, Ryan Dancy, Sergii Strelchuk
problem: Whether a graph has some property does not depend on how its vertices are numbered, yet most algorithms use the numbering. A circuit is called symmetric if every renumbering of the vertices extends to a rearrangement of the circuit itself. For classical circuits this restriction is strong enough to prove unconditional lower bounds, a rare thing in complexity theory. Can the same be done for quantum circuits, and which quantum resource has to be limited for such a bound to hold?
result: Entanglement is the resource. Let the entanglement width of a circuit be the smallest \(b\) such that, on every classical input and after every layer, the state is a product of blocks of at most \(b\) qubits. There is an explicit graph property, decidable in classical polynomial time, that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width \(o(n/\log n)\) computes, with arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates and any depth. More generally, width \(O(n/f(n))\) excludes size \(2^{o(f(n))}\) for every \(f\) growing faster than \(\log n\). Without the width restriction, symmetric circuits of polynomial size compute every graph property in BQP. With width one, hence no entanglement, they already compute every property definable in fixed-point logic with counting.
significance: The theorem is an unconditional lower bound that applies to quantum circuits with unlimited depth, and it applies to a problem that is easy. It locates where the power of symmetric quantum computation comes from: to solve this problem without choosing a vertex order, the circuit must entangle almost as many qubits as there are vertices. The converse statements show that the restriction is meaningful in both directions, since too little entanglement still gives a large logical class and unrestricted entanglement gives everything.
limitations: Symmetry of the circuit is the assumption that makes the proof work; the bound says nothing about general circuits, for which the problem is easy classically. Width is measured between layers of commuting gates and only on computational-basis inputs. Whether linear width is needed, and whether any constant width gives exactly fixed-point logic with counting, are left as an open question and a conjecture. The authors disclose that the pebble game and the lower bounds were obtained and written without AI assistance, and that Theorems 1.4–1.6 (the BQP simulation, the entanglement-free simulation and the symmetric QAOA circuit) were later obtained by Google Antigravity when they prompted it, and then simplified and rewritten by them.

description: A graph on \(n\) vertices is fed in as \(n^2\) qubits, one for each ordered pair, in a computational-basis state; further qubits start in \(\ket0\). Gates act on one or two qubits and are grouped into layers of commuting gates. The circuit is symmetric if every permutation of the vertices, acting on the input wires, can be extended to a permutation of all wires that maps each layer to itself and fixes the output wire. Nothing forbids a large workspace that is itself permuted.

Classically this model is tied to logic. Anderson and Dawar showed that polynomial-size symmetric circuits with threshold gates compute exactly the properties definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Cai, Fürer and Immerman constructed pairs of graphs that this logic cannot tell apart, although a simple polynomial-time algorithm can. The hard property of the paper is built from those pairs, padded with isolated vertices so that they remain indistinguishable when only even permutations are required.

Indistinguishability is phrased as a game. Spoiler marks vertices with pebbles, and Duplicator answers with a renumbering that respects the marks; Spoiler wins when the marked parts of the two graphs differ. The new game allows quantum inputs: instead of comparing marked subgraphs it compares reduced density matrices on the qubits that the pebbles pin down. On classical inputs it reproduces the classical game. The main theorem says that if a circuit has small supports, in the sense that fixing few vertices fixes any small tuple of wires, and Duplicator wins with twice as many pebbles, then the circuit accepts both graphs with exactly the same probability.

Entanglement enters because a gate cannot be analysed from the reduced states of single wires. If the state after each layer is a product of blocks of at most \(b\) qubits, the reduced states of \(b\)-tuples of wires determine it, and the argument can follow tuples instead of wires. Larger tuples have larger supports, so the number of pebbles grows with \(b\). The classical pairs stay indistinguishable up to a number of pebbles linear in \(n\), and the trade-off between size and width follows.

The upper bounds show what the restriction costs. To simulate any quantum algorithm symmetrically, the circuit prepares a superposition of labels for the vertices, sorts the vertices by label, and runs the algorithm on the sorted graph. The result is the original acceptance probability averaged over orderings, at an extra cost of \(O(n^4\log^2n)\) gates. A symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, whose acceptance probability equals the probability that QAOA satisfies at least \(t\) equations, is offered as a starting point for entanglement lower bounds in optimization.

methods.technique: From circuit size to small supports to few pebbles
methods.explanation: The only thing that size does is limit how many wires there are, hence how many different images a tuple of wires can have under renumberings. A theorem on permutation groups turns few images into a small set of vertices that controls the tuple, and those vertices are where Spoiler puts pebbles.
math: Let \([\vec w]\) be a tuple of \(\ell\) distinct wires up to the internal symmetries of the circuit. Wires that no gate touches can be exchanged freely, so with \(s\) two-qubit gates at most \(2s+1\) ancilla wires matter, and the number of images of \([\vec w]\) under all even renumberings is at most \[\bigl(\max\{2s+1,\,n^2\}\bigr)^{\ell}.\]

If this number is smaller than \(\binom nk\) with \(k\le n/4\), a theorem on subgroups of the alternating group gives a set \(S\) of fewer than \(k\) vertices such that every even permutation fixing \(S\) pointwise fixes \([\vec w]\). Since \(\binom{n}{k-1}\ge2^{k-1}\) in this range, the support size is at most the base-two logarithm of the number of images, \[|S|\le\ell\,\log_2\max\{2s+1,n^2\}.\]

The indistinguishability theorem needs \(2|S|\) pebbles, and the hard pairs tolerate \(k_n=\Theta(n)\). With \(\ell\) equal to the entanglement width, a circuit that tells the pair apart must satisfy \[s>2^{\min\{k_n/2,\;n/4-1\}/\ell-1}-\tfrac12\] for infinitely many \(n\). Width \(\ell=O(n/f(n))\) makes the exponent of order \(f(n)\), which is the statement of the main theorem; \(f=\omega(\log n)\) covers all polynomial sizes.
methods.transfer: The chain "few images, small support, few pebbles" works for any circuit model in which the action of a layer on a small part of the state is determined by small parts before it. Tensor networks with symmetric contraction schemes, symmetric arithmetic circuits and equivariant neural networks are natural candidates. What must be supplied in each case is the reconstruction step, which here is the bounded block size.

methods.technique: Following a discrepancy backwards through a layer
methods.explanation: To prove that two inputs give the same output, assume that they do not and let Spoiler trace the discrepancy from the output wire to the input. At each layer a difference in the reduced state of some tuple of wires must come from a difference in some tuple before the layer, and the symmetry of the layer lets Spoiler find it with a bounded number of pebbles. The converse side of the paper uses a simple trick to count without entangling, which we illustrate for parity.
math: For a state \(\rho\) let \(f_\rho(\vec w)\) be its reduced state on the ordered tuple \(\vec w\). A layer has partition symmetry if, for each \(\vec w\), the set of all \(\ell\)-tuples splits into classes with the following property. Symmetries of the circuit that fix \(\vec w\) preserve the classes. And if the values of \(f\) before the layer agree up to rearrangement inside the classes, for two pure states of width at most \(\ell\), then the reduced states on \(\vec w\) after the layer agree. The paper proves that layers of one- and two-qubit gates always have this property at \(\ell\) equal to the width.

Suppose the reduced states on \(\vec w\) differ after the layer, for every extension of the current renumbering. Then in some class, and in some orbit inside it, no rearrangement matches the values before the layer. Spoiler places pebbles on the support of a tuple in that orbit, one by one. At each step Duplicator's answer only permutes the orbit, so the mismatch persists on a smaller orbit. After at most \(k\) rounds the orbit is a single class of tuples and a definite \(\vec w'\) with differing reduced states remains. Repeating this to the first layer contradicts that the initial encoded graphs agree on pebbled qubits.

Counting without entanglement (editorial). Put one counter qubit in \(\ket+\) and apply \(CZ\) between it and every edge qubit. On a basis input the edge qubits are classical, so each gate is either nothing or a \(Z\) on the counter, and the state stays a product, \[\ket{x}\otimes\ket+\ \longmapsto\ \ket{x}\otimes\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0+(-1)^{|x|}\ket1\bigr).\] A Hadamard then reveals the parity of the number of edges. The layer is invariant under renumbering and has width one. The paper notes that polynomial-size symmetric circuits with ordinary Boolean gates cannot compute this parity. Phases on a register of several counter qubits, followed by an inverse Fourier transform, give the full count and hence threshold gates.
methods.transfer: Backward tracing of reduced-state differences is a general way to prove that a structured quantum circuit cannot separate two inputs, with no need to bound its depth. It should adapt to other symmetry groups, provided they have good support theorems. The counting trick is useful whenever a symmetric circuit must aggregate many classical bits into a fixed register without entangling them.
